title: Eviction Policies
summary: LRU and its alternatives — how a cache decides what to throw away once memory runs out, and why that choice quietly shapes hit ratio.

slides.markdown:
A cache has finite memory, so it can't just keep growing forever — at some point something has to be thrown out to make room for something new. The rule that decides *what* gets thrown out is an **eviction policy**.

This is not a minor implementation detail: the wrong policy for a given access pattern can tank a cache's hit ratio even though the cache itself is working exactly as designed. This topic covers LRU (the default), its main alternatives, and how it's actually implemented under the hood.

slides.sectionTitle: Why eviction is unavoidable: bounded memory
slides.markdown:
A cache trades memory for speed, and memory is always finite — a Redis instance might have 16GB of RAM, but the data it *could* cache (every product, every user profile, every search result) can easily be far larger than that. Once the cache is full, adding a new entry means something existing has to go.

This is true no matter how well-designed the cache is — it isn't a bug to fix, it's a permanent constraint. The only real design choice is *which* entry gets evicted, since that choice determines whether the cache keeps holding data that's actually still useful.

A cache with a bad eviction policy for its workload behaves like a cache that's too small, even if the hardware is generous.

slides.sectionTitle: LRU: the default choice and how it's implemented
slides.markdown:
**LRU** (Least Recently Used) evicts whichever entry hasn't been accessed for the longest time, on the theory that data used recently is likely to be used again soon — a pattern real workloads often follow (this is called **temporal locality**).

It's the default in most caching systems (Redis, Memcached, browser caches) because it needs no configuration and performs well across a wide range of access patterns without any tuning.

The intuition: think of a stack of papers on a desk. Every time you use one, it goes back on top. When the desk is full, you clear out from the bottom — the paper you haven't touched in the longest time.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: LRU via hashmap + doubly linked list
slides.markdown:
![LRU cache hashmap paired with a doubly linked list](assets/lru-structure.svg)

The classic LRU implementation pairs a **hashmap** (key to the exact node holding that value, for O(1) lookup) with a **doubly linked list** ordered from most-recently-used at the head to least-recently-used at the tail.

On every access, the accessed node is unlinked and moved to the head. When the cache is full, the tail node — the true least-recently-used entry — is unlinked and removed, and its key is deleted from the hashmap too.

assets.alt: LRU cache hashmap paired with a doubly linked list

slides.sectionTitle: LFU and FIFO: when they beat LRU
slides.markdown:
LRU isn't always the right fit. **LFU** (Least Frequently Used) evicts the entry with the *fewest total accesses*, not just the one used least recently — it beats LRU when some items are consistently hot over a long period, since LRU can evict a very popular item just because of one recent quiet stretch. **FIFO** evicts whatever was inserted first, regardless of usage — simplest to implement, but it ignores access patterns entirely.

| Policy | Evicts | Best for | Weak point |
|---|---|---|---|
| LRU | Least recently accessed | General-purpose, recency-biased workloads | Vulnerable to one-off scans (next slide's pitfall) |
| LFU | Least frequently accessed | Long-term popularity (e.g. viral content) | Slow to adapt when popularity shifts |
| FIFO | Oldest inserted | Simple queues, when access pattern doesn't matter | Ignores usage entirely — can evict hot data |

**How to decide:** default to LRU; switch to LFU when you specifically expect a stable set of "always popular" items that shouldn't be evicted by a burst of unrelated traffic.

**TTL** (time-to-live) expiry and eviction solve different problems and usually run together. TTL says "this entry is no longer trustworthy after N seconds, regardless of memory pressure" — it's about correctness and freshness. Eviction says "we're out of room, remove something" — it's about capacity.

A cache entry can be removed for either reason: it can expire via TTL even with plenty of free memory (protecting against stale data), or it can be evicted under an LRU/LFU policy even before its TTL is up (protecting against running out of memory).

In practice, most production caches set both: a TTL as a correctness backstop, and an eviction policy as a memory backstop — neither one alone covers both concerns.

slides.sectionTitle: Approximated LRU at scale (Redis' sampling approach)
slides.markdown:
True LRU requires tracking exact access order for every key, which costs memory and CPU per access — at millions of keys, that bookkeeping adds up. Redis instead uses **approximated LRU**: it samples a small random set of keys (a handful by default) and evicts the least-recently-used *among that sample*, rather than the true least-recently-used across the whole keyspace.

This trades a small amount of eviction accuracy for a large reduction in overhead, and in practice performs close to true LRU — increasing the sample size makes it more accurate at the cost of a bit more CPU per eviction.

The lesson generalizes: at large scale, an approximate version of a policy that's cheap to run often beats an exact version that's too expensive to run on every operation.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: LRU cache with get/put in O(1)
slides.markdown:
A hashmap of key to node, plus a doubly linked list, gives O(1) `get` and `put`:

```python
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = {}  # key -> Node
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()  # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        node = self.cache[key]
        self._move_to_front(node)
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.cache:
            self._remove(self.cache[key])
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.cache[key] = node
        self._add_to_front(node)
        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.cache[lru.key]
```

Every operation — lookup, move-to-front, evict-the-tail — is a constant number of pointer updates, which is exactly why the hashmap-plus-linked-list combination is the standard answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: LRU thrashing under a scan-heavy access pattern
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "LRU always keeps the data that matters most, since it's based on recency."

**Why it's wrong:** a single large sequential scan — a batch job reading every row in a table once — touches every key exactly once and marks each as "most recently used." That scan can evict an entire cache full of genuinely hot, frequently-reused data, replacing it with data that will likely never be read again.

**Correct model:** LRU assumes recent access predicts future access, which fails for one-off scans. Mitigations include using LFU for workloads where scans are common, or giving scan-triggered reads a separate, smaller cache region so they can't evict the main working set.
